questions.question: For which size of matrix is Sarrus' rule intended?
options: Only for $2\times2$ matrices.
For every square matrix.
Only for $3\times3$ matrices.
Only for diagonal matrices.

questions.question: In Sarrus' rule, which diagonal products receive positive signs?
options: All six diagonal products.
The three falling diagonal products.
The three rising diagonal products.
Only the main diagonal product.

questions.question: What is subtracted when applying Sarrus' rule?
options: The products along the falling diagonals.
The diagonal entries themselves.
The sum of all off-diagonal entries.
The products along the rising diagonals.

questions.question: Why is Sarrus' rule best treated as a mnemonic rather than a general determinant theorem?
options: It works only when every entry is positive.
It gives eigenvalues rather than determinants.
Its diagonal trick does not extend to larger matrices
It requires the matrix to be symmetric.

questions.question: A student wants to compute a $4\times4$ determinant by copying the first columns and drawing diagonals as in Sarrus' rule. What is the main problem?
options: Only row operations can define a determinant.
The Sarrus diagonal shortcut is not valid for $4\times4$ determinants.
A $4\times4$ matrix has no determinant.
The determinant must be positive for a $4\times4$ matrix.

questions.question: Using Sarrus' rule on $I_3$, what determinant do you get?
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}$, what does Sarrus' rule give for $\det(A)$?
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\1&2&3\\0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$, what should Sarrus' rule give?
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&3\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\det(A)$?
In Sarrus' rule for $\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i\end{pmatrix}$, which product is one of the positive products?
options: $aei$
$ceg$
$afh$
$bdi$

questions.question: Why does Sarrus' rule have six triple products for a $3\times3$ matrix?
options: A determinant always has twice as many terms as rows.
There are six entries outside the main diagonal.
Three falling diagonal products and three rising ones
Each row is multiplied by every column entry once.

questions.question: When comparing Sarrus' rule with cofactor expansion for a $3\times3$ determinant, what is true?
options: Sarrus' rule changes the value when rows are swapped.
Sarrus' rule computes the trace instead.
Cofactor expansion only works for diagonal matrices.
They give the same determinant, organised differently

questions.question: What should you check before using Sarrus' rule in a calculation?
options: That the matrix is exactly $3\times3$.
That all entries are nonzero.
That the matrix is already diagonal.
That the matrix has determinant $1$.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&4\\5&6&0\end{pmatrix}$, Sarrus' rule gives which determinant?
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\3&1&0\\0&4&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\det(A)$ using Sarrus' rule?
In the Sarrus formula for $\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i\end{pmatrix}$, which pair has opposite signs?
options: $aei$ is negative and $ceg$ is positive.
$afh$ is positive and $bdi$ is negative.
$bfg$ is negative and $cdh$ is positive.
$aei$ is positive and $ceg$ is negative.

questions.question: Why can a matrix with two equal rows be a good quick check on a Sarrus computation?
options: The determinant should equal the trace.
The determinant should be zero, so the products must cancel
The determinant should equal the sum of the equal row.
The determinant should become undefined.

questions.question: A student says Sarrus' rule is easier, so it should replace cofactor expansion entirely. What is the precise objection?
options: Sarrus' rule gives approximate determinants.
Sarrus' rule is not a general method beyond $3\times3$ matrices.
Sarrus' rule works only for invertible matrices.
Cofactor expansion only gives signs, not values.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&1\\3&-1&4\\5&0&2\end{pmatrix}$, what determinant is obtained by Sarrus' rule?
A Sarrus computation gives positive diagonal sum $18$ and rising diagonal sum $23$. What is the determinant?
